scenes.title: What can one angle hide?
scenes.narration: Can one X-ray angle hide a narrowed artery? Look at this simulated angiogram. A nearby branch overlaps the area. When the view changes, the same narrowing is easier to see.

scenes.title: What the image shows
scenes.narration: A coronary angiogram is a moving X-ray study of the arteries that feed the heart muscle. Contrast enters through a catheter and outlines the channel that blood can pass through. The team watches the moving images to trace each artery and look for changes in the outline.

scenes.title: Follow the branches
scenes.narration: The team identifies the main branches before deciding where a narrowing is. In this example, the left main artery divides into the left anterior descending artery and the circumflex. A separate view shows the right coronary artery. Following the branches helps the team describe the exact location of a finding.

scenes.title: Spot the narrowing
scenes.narration: Here is one short narrowing. Contrast still passes through it and reaches the artery beyond. The team compares the narrowest part with a nearby reference segment and describes where the narrowing is, how long it is, and how severe it looks. A narrowing and a complete blockage look different on the images.

scenes.title: Why the team changes angle
scenes.narration: The X-ray turns three-dimensional arteries into a flat image. From one angle, branches can overlap or a segment can look shorter than it is. A second view can separate the branches and show more of the same narrowing. The clinician compares the recordings before describing what they see.

scenes.title: Does it affect blood supply?
scenes.narration: The size of a narrowing on the picture gives the team one part of the answer. If its effect on blood supply is unclear, the team may use a thin pressure-sensing wire. Tests called F F R or I F R compare pressure beyond the narrowing with pressure upstream. The results help guide treatment decisions.

scenes.title: When major arteries look open
scenes.narration: Sometimes the major arteries show no important blockage, even though a person has symptoms. Small blood vessels can work poorly, or a coronary artery can tighten temporarily. The care team uses the symptoms and other findings to decide whether more tests could help explain what is happening.

scenes.title: How the findings guide care
scenes.narration: The result goes into a larger decision. The team considers the symptoms, urgency, which arteries are involved and any other tests. Care may include medicines and prevention, further assessment, a catheter procedure such as angioplasty and stenting, or a discussion about bypass surgery. In a heart attack, decisions may need to happen quickly.

scenes.title: Three questions about the result
scenes.narration: When the team explains an angiogram, three questions can make the result easier to understand. Which artery was involved? Is there evidence that the narrowing affects blood supply? What follow-up or treatment does the team recommend? Those answers connect the picture to a plan for care.
